title: D.1 Gravitation
subject: IBDP Physics
introduction: Gravitation is the force every mass exerts on every other mass, and the field is the way that influence is described at a distance. This lesson builds from the inverse-square law to field strength, then applies both to orbits — why a satellite stays up, what sets its speed, and how Kepler’s laws follow from Newton’s.
learning_objectives: Understand the concept of a field as action at a distance.
Apply the concept of gravitational field strength.
Explain orbital motion using centripetal force.
Use Kepler’s laws of planetary motion.
Apply gravitational potential and potential energy (HL).

definitions.meaning: A region of space where an object experiences a force due to another object or source.
The gravitational force per unit mass at a point, in N kg⁻¹, numerically equal to the free-fall acceleration.
A line showing the direction of the force on a test object, with closer spacing indicating a stronger field.
The work done per unit mass to bring a small mass from infinity to a point, defined as zero at infinity and therefore always negative.
The launch speed at which an object just reaches infinity with no kinetic energy remaining.
An equatorial orbit with a period of exactly one day, so the satellite stays above the same point on the Earth’s surface.

core_concepts.heading: Field Interactions
core_concepts.explanation: Fields allow objects to interact without touching. A source object creates a field, and another object experiences a force when placed within that field.

core_concepts.heading: Field Lines
core_concepts.explanation: Field lines show the direction of force. Closer field lines represent stronger fields, while wider spacing represents weaker fields.

core_concepts.heading: Uniform Fields
core_concepts.explanation: A uniform field has constant strength and direction throughout a region. Parallel and equally spaced field lines represent a uniform field.

core_concepts.heading: Inverse Square Relationship
core_concepts.explanation: Many fields become weaker as distance from the source increases. Gravitational and electric fields follow inverse square relationships.

gravitational_fields.explanation: Gravitational field strength describes the force experienced by a unit mass placed in a gravitational field.
A mass creates a gravitational field around it. The field becomes weaker as distance from the mass increases.
Gravitational potential is the work done per unit mass when moving a small mass from infinity to a point in the field.

worked_examples.question: The gravitational field strength at the surface of a planet is 3.7 N kg⁻¹. Calculate the weight of a 60 kg astronaut standing on it.
worked_examples.answer: 222 N, which is about a fifth of their weight on Earth

worked_examples.question: Calculate the gravitational field strength at a point where a 10 kg mass experiences a force of 98 N.
A satellite orbits 400 km above the Earth’s surface. Taking the Earth’s radius as 6.37 × 10⁶ m and GM = 3.99 × 10¹⁴ m³ s⁻², calculate its orbital speed.
solution: The orbital radius is measured from the centre: r = 6.37 × 10⁶ + 4.00 × 10⁵ = 6.77 × 10⁶ m

field_diagrams.explanation: Gravitational field lines point towards the centre of mass because gravity is always attractive. The spacing of lines shows field strength.

satellite_motion.explanation: Satellites remain in orbit because gravitational force provides the centripetal force required for circular motion.
Orbital speed depends on the mass of the object being orbited and the distance from its centre.
A geostationary satellite has the same angular velocity as Earth and appears fixed above one location.

real_world_applications: Power generators use electromagnetic induction to produce electricity.
Electric motors use magnetic forces to create motion.
Satellites use gravitational fields for orbital movement.
Transformers use changing magnetic fields to transfer electrical energy.
Medical MRI machines use strong magnetic fields.
common_mistakes: Confusing gravitational field strength with gravitational potential — one is force per unit mass, the other energy per unit mass.
Measuring r from the surface of a planet instead of from its centre.
Forgetting that gravitational potential and potential energy are negative, because they are defined as zero at infinity.
Using the 1/r² dependence for potential; the field goes as 1/r² but the potential goes as 1/r.
Thinking a satellite in a lower orbit moves more slowly — it actually moves faster, though it has less total energy.
Assuming escape speed depends on the mass of the escaping object; it does not.
ib_exam_tips: Always measure r from the centre of the body, adding the planetary radius to any stated altitude.
State that gravity provides the centripetal force before equating the two expressions in an orbit question.
Draw gravitational field lines pointing inwards, since gravity is only ever attractive.
Keep the negative sign on potential and potential energy.
Check the powers: field and force go as 1/r², potential and potential energy as 1/r.

hl_extension.explanation: Energy per unit mass, zero at infinity and negative everywhere else because work must be done to escape.
The negative value shows the pair is bound; a bound orbit has negative total energy.
Found by setting the total energy to zero. Independent of the escaping object’s mass.

practice_questions.question: State what a gravitational field line represents.
practice_questions.answer: The direction of the gravitational force on a small test mass, with closer spacing showing a stronger field.

practice_questions.question: Why do satellites remain in orbit around the Earth?
practice_questions.answer: Gravity provides exactly the centripetal force required for circular motion at that radius, so the satellite continually falls towards the Earth while moving fast enough sideways to keep missing it.

practice_questions.question: Explain why the gravitational field strength at the top of a mountain is slightly less than at sea level.
practice_questions.answer: Field strength is GM/r² and r is measured from the centre of the Earth. At the top of a mountain r is larger, so g is smaller.

practice_questions.question: Explain why a satellite in a lower orbit travels faster yet has less total energy.
practice_questions.answer: Orbital speed is √(GM/r), which increases as r falls. Total energy is −GMm/2r, which becomes more negative as r falls, so the total energy is lower despite the greater speed.

summary: Fields explain how objects interact without direct contact. Gravitational, electric and magnetic fields are used to describe forces, energy transfer and motion. These concepts are important for understanding satellites, electricity generation, motors and modern technology.

formulas.name: Newton's Law of Gravitation
formulas.explanation: Always attractive, and r is measured centre to centre, not from the surface.

formulas.name: Gravitational Field Strength

variables.g: field strength (N kg⁻¹, equivalently m s⁻²)

formulas.explanation: Force per unit mass, numerically equal to the free-fall acceleration.

formulas.name: Orbital Speed
formulas.explanation: From setting the gravitational force equal to the centripetal force.

formulas.name: Kepler's Third Law
formulas.explanation: The square of the period is proportional to the cube of the orbital radius.

formulas.name: Gravitational Potential
formulas.explanation: Energy per unit mass, defined as zero at infinity and therefore negative everywhere else.

formulas.name: Gravitational Potential Energy
formulas.explanation: Note the 1/r dependence, against 1/r² for the force.

formulas.name: Escape Speed
formulas.explanation: The launch speed that just reaches infinity with no energy to spare. Independent of the escaping object’s mass.
